HIBEAM/ANNIE2, aims to detect free neutrons resulting from neutrino interactions deep within the Earth's atmosphere. To achieve this goal, researchers are designing a massive, 400-tonne detector with an extremely thin (~50% rock) layer of water in the atmosphere in front of it. A key challenge lies in distinguishing between atmospheric muons and neutrino-induced muons, and a novel approach involves using a combination of Cherenkov and scintillating materials to identify and track all muons generated during interactions. To further refine the free-neutron detection sensitivity, an updated version of the HIBEAM/ANNIE2 experiment is being explored, involving a 1 km^2 large array of vertical, finely-spaced strings (~1 cm spacing) with modular modules (consisting of 5 m long, 1 m^2) composed of scintillating counters and Cherenov tubes. This upgraded setup will provide a significantly larger target area for neutrino interactions, enhanced muon tracking capabilities, and a reduced background from cosmic rays, thus enabling the detection of a neutrino flux ~100 times lower than initially anticipated. The upgraded experiment, known as HIBEAM-PLUS, is currently under review and development, with a focus on optimizing its design to achieve the desired sensitivity while keeping costs relatively low. To this end, researchers are exploring the use of off-the-shelf, affordable components, and a detailed layout of the large array. A simulation-based study of the upgraded HIBEAM-PLUS design has been conducted, and its effectiveness in achieving the desired sensitivity has been demonstrated. imeter data is a crucial task in oceanography.  A novel approach using wavelet analysis is introduced to model the roughness of the altimeter data. This study introduces the LHC-MLv2 framework, a machine learning tool designed to handle increased luminosity without retraining, by utilizing a hierarchical training process. This involves training a basic model on a small dataset, followed by the generation of a set of synthetic data points that are used to train a more advanced model. This advanced model can then be used to make accurate predictions, even when confronted with significantly larger datasets. This hierarchical training process enables the creation of a library of models that can accommodate different luminosity levels, allowing for seamless integration into existing analysis pipelines.
